Inside, the old magnate was oblivious to the storm. He lay sprawled behind his mahogany desk, a single, dark stain blooming on the pristine white of his shirt, a heavy silver letter opener lying inches from his outstretched hand. The scream that tore through the oppressive silence belonged to Eleanor, his young wife, who stood framed in the doorway, her face a mask of porcelain horror.

Her cry was answered by thundering footsteps from the adjoining billiards room. Arthur Vance, Alistair’s long-suffering business partner, burst in, his face ashen and his usually immaculate tie slightly askew. He stopped short, his eyes wide, taking in the scene with a choked gasp. Moments later, Beatrice Blackwood, Alistair's stern, older sister, appeared at the top of the grand staircase, her descent slow and deliberate. Her gaze, cold as the marble floor, swept over the scene before settling not on her brother’s body, but on Arthur’s panicked face.

It was less than half an hour before Detective Inspector Corbin arrived, his trench coat dripping onto the pristine oriental rug. He was a weary but sharp-eyed man, admitted by a stoic butler, Jennings, whose loyalty to the Blackwood name seemed as old and cracked as the manor’s foundations. Corbin took in the scene with a practiced glance: the weeping widow, the pacing business partner, the statuesque sister. "Nobody leaves this house," he stated, his voice calm but carrying an undeniable authority. "I'll need to speak with each of you individually."

Corbin began his examination of the study, his movements methodical and quiet. He knelt beside Alistair’s body, noting the position of the letter opener and the lack of any obvious signs of a struggle on the desk itself. His gaze swept the room, cataloguing the expensive books, the decanters of amber liquid, the cold hearth. Then, his eyes caught a glint of gold near the heavy velvet drapes that concealed the rain-lashed French doors. Using his pen, he carefully nudged a small, circular object from beneath the fabric: a cufflink, engraved with the ornate, unmistakable initials 'A.V.'

With a delicate maneuver, Corbin dropped the cufflink into a small evidence bag, his face an impassive mask. His attention then shifted to the French doors themselves. He ran a gloved finger along the brass handle, noting that the bolt was not thrown—a detail that suggested either a hurried exit or an expected arrival. From across the room, he saw Arthur Vance stiffen, the man's gaze darting from the detective's actions near the window to his own wrist, where a matching cufflink gleamed under the lamplight. A single bead of sweat traced a path down Arthur’s temple.

"Mr. Vance, if you would," Corbin said, his voice cutting through the tense silence. He gestured towards the library across the hall, its leather-bound books casting long shadows in the dim light. Arthur swallowed hard, his Adam's apple bobbing, and followed the detective, his posture stiff and defensive. "You and Mr. Blackwood had a disagreement recently, I'm told," Corbin began, foregoing any pleasantries as he leaned against a heavy oak desk. Arthur flinched, his eyes wide. "That's a gross oversimplification," he stammered. "We had a... a difference of professional opinion regarding the new merger. Alistair was being reckless, risking everything we'd built!" His voice rose with agitation, betraying a depth of frustration that felt far more personal than professional.

Corbin remained silent for a moment, letting Arthur’s agitated words fill the space between them. "And this merger," the detective continued, his tone deceptively casual, "would it have benefited you financially if Alistair had... backed out? Or was removed from the equation entirely?" Arthur paled, the accusation hanging unspoken in the air. "It would have ruined me!" he retorted, his voice cracking. "Alistair held the majority shares. His refusal to sign meant the deal would collapse, taking my entire personal fortune with it. I was trying to save us, not destroy him!"

Leaving a shaken Arthur Vance in the library, Corbin sought out Eleanor, the young widow. He found her in the drawing-room, huddled in a large armchair, clutching a silk handkerchief. Her sobs had subsided into quiet, shuddering breaths. "Mrs. Blackwood," Corbin began gently, "I know this is difficult, but can you tell me what you saw?" Eleanor looked up, her blue eyes swimming with tears. "I... I was coming to bring Alistair his evening tea. He always took it at nine. The door was ajar, and I saw... I saw him," she choked out, a fresh wave of grief washing over her. "Before that," Corbin pressed, "did you hear anything? Voices? An argument?" She shook her head. "No, just... just Arthur. He was with Alistair earlier, in the study. Their voices were raised. It sounded terrible."

Corbin thanked the grieving widow and made his way to Beatrice Blackwood's private sitting room. She sat bolt upright in a high-backed chair, her hands folded primly in her lap, showing none of the emotional turmoil of the others. "My brother was a fool in business and a fool in love," she stated without preamble, her voice as brittle as dry leaves. "He trusted Arthur, a man whose ambition has always outstripped his talent. And he married that... that girl, who was clearly only after his money." Her eyes narrowed. "I warned him about Arthur just this afternoon. I told him I'd seen the man tampering with the safe in the study last week. Alistair just laughed it off."

The mention of the safe piqued Corbin's interest. He returned to the study, the scene now illuminated by the harsh glare of a portable police lamp. He located the safe, cleverly concealed behind a large oil painting of a grim-faced ancestor. Running a gloved finger along the dial, he found it cold and undisturbed, but noted several deep scratches near the combination dial, fresh gouges in the dark metal that seemed to corroborate Beatrice's claim of tampering. It was a lock that would require skill or force to open, and the marks suggested a failed, frustrated attempt.

Corbin then turned his attention to the desk. He meticulously sorted through the stacks of paper, most of them business documents and ledgers. Tucked beneath a blotting pad, however, he found something different. It was a single sheet of embossed letterhead from a prestigious law firm, dated just two days prior. The text was brief and formal, confirming an appointment for Alistair Blackwood to make significant alterations to his last will and testament. The appointment was for the following morning.

With this new piece of information, Corbin decided to press Arthur Vance again. He found the man pacing relentlessly in the billiards room, his face a mask of anxiety. "Changing his will," Arthur scoffed when Corbin presented the letter. "Of course he was. He was planning to write me out completely, all because I wouldn't support his disastrous merger. He told me as much during our argument. He said by tomorrow, I wouldn't be worth the ink on his signature." His hands clenched into tight fists at his sides, his knuckles white with fury.

The pieces were beginning to form a damning picture, and Arthur Vance was at its center. A man on the brink of financial ruin, facing complete disinheritance, who had argued violently with the victim just hours before his death. His cufflink was found at the scene, near a potentially unlocked escape route. Beatrice claimed he'd been trying to crack the safe, and Eleanor overheard their heated confrontation. It was a classic case of greed and desperation, almost too neat, too textbook. Yet, Corbin couldn't shake a feeling of unease, a nagging sense that one of the brushstrokes in this grim portrait was out of place.

Corbin decided to re-examine the murder weapon. The silver letter opener was heavy, ornate, and now stained with Alistair's blood. He carefully inspected the handle, a twisted design of ivy leaves. Within the intricate metalwork, almost completely obscured by the dark, drying blood, he spotted it: a single, long strand of blonde hair, caught tightly in a crevice of the silver. It was a detail easily missed, a pale thread against the gleaming metal.

Holding the evidence bag containing the hair up to the light, Corbin's mind raced. Arthur Vance's hair was dark and receding. Beatrice's was a severe, iron-grey bun. Alistair himself had been mostly bald. That left Eleanor, the beautiful, weeping, blonde widow. It was a jarring contradiction to the mountain of evidence pointing squarely at Arthur. Could she have been involved? Or was it merely a stray hair, transferred from an embrace or a shared moment earlier in the day? The simplicity of the motive against Arthur warred with the stark physical evidence in his hand.

Corbin requested to see Eleanor's chambers. She granted permission with a listless wave of her hand. The room was a stark contrast to the rest of the manor; modern, airy, and filled with light colors. On her vanity table, amidst an array of perfumes and silver-backed brushes, lay a small, velvet-lined jewelry box. The detective, with her permission, opened it. Inside, nestled amongst pearls and diamonds, was a collection of exquisite, antique cufflinks, a hobby she'd apparently curated for her husband. At least, that's what one would assume.

He returned to Eleanor in the drawing room, holding the evidence bag with the single strand of hair. "Mrs. Blackwood, this was found on the murder weapon," he said, his voice neutral. She visibly recoiled, her hand flying to her mouth. "That's... that's impossible," she whispered, her eyes wide with what looked like genuine shock and fear. "I was nowhere near... I loved my husband. Why would I...?" Her composure finally shattered, and she dissolved into heaving, desperate sobs.

Corbin left her to her grief, the performance, if it was one, utterly convincing. He found Jennings, the butler, polishing silver in the pantry, his movements slow and methodical. "Jennings," Corbin began, "you've been with this family a long time. Tell me about Mrs. Blackwood. The first Mrs. Blackwood." The butler paused, his polishing cloth held mid-air. "Ah, Clara," he said, a ghost of a smile touching his thin lips. "She passed ten years ago. A lovely woman. Fair-haired, like the current Mrs. Blackwood. Alistair never truly got over her. He kept all her things, just as she left them."

"And where are her things kept, Jennings?" Corbin asked, a new theory beginning to crystallize in his mind. The butler gestured with his head towards the upper floors. "In the old west wing, sir. Untouched for a decade. Mr. Blackwood couldn't bear to have them cleared out. He called it her 'memory room'." Corbin felt a jolt of understanding. A blonde hair didn't have to belong to a living blonde. It could be a memento, a remnant from a place steeped in the past.

With Jennings' key, Corbin entered the west wing, a layer of dust covering everything like a fine shroud. The 'memory room' was just as the butler described it; a suite of rooms preserved in time. A woman's dressing gown lay across a chair, and on the vanity, a silver-backed brush lay untouched. Corbin carefully examined the brush. It was filled with long, blonde hairs, identical in color and texture to the one he'd found on the letter opener. He realized the hair wasn't a clue to the killer's identity, but to the victim's state of mind.

He returned to the study and stood over the body, the pieces of the puzzle now rearranging themselves into a completely different picture. The letter opener lay near Alistair's hand, not gripped within it. The note about the will, the fierce argument with Arthur—it wasn't a prelude to murder, but to something else entirely. Alistair, facing financial ruin from a bad deal and haunted by the memory of his first wife, was a man in despair. Corbin now saw the scene not as a homicide, but as a meticulously staged suicide, designed to look like anything but.

But a staged suicide still needs a stage manager. Someone had to plant the cufflink, scratch the safe, and subtly guide the narrative. Who benefited most from Arthur Vance being framed for murder? Not Eleanor, who would simply inherit. Not Arthur himself, obviously. His eyes settled on the figure standing silently in the hall, watching him with an unnerving stillness. Beatrice Blackwood. She had despised her brother's new wife and his business partner. With Alistair dead and Arthur imprisoned, the entire Blackwood fortune, every last share and title, would revert to the only remaining blood relative: her.

"Miss Blackwood," Corbin called out, his voice echoing in the grand hall. Beatrice turned her head slowly, her expression unreadable. "It was a clever plan. My brother kills himself, despondent over his failing business and his dead wife, but you couldn't let it be that simple, could you?" He walked towards her, his steps deliberate. "You saw your chance to get rid of the two people you despised most. You took Arthur's cufflink from his coat when he rushed in, dropping it by the window. You invented the story about the safe to cement his motive of greed. You ensured we saw him as a desperate, violent man."

Beatrice’s cold composure finally cracked, a flicker of fury animating her stone-like features. "My brother was a weak fool who was squandering our family's legacy on a gold-digging harlot and a feckless partner!" she spat, her voice laced with a lifetime of resentment. "He was going to ruin us all. His suicide was a final act of cowardice, but it presented an opportunity. Arthur was the perfect scapegoat. It was a fitting end, tidying up all of my brother's loose ends in one fell swoop." She didn't confess to murder, but to manipulation, a crime of cold, calculating opportunism.

Corbin shook his head slowly. "You almost got away with it," he conceded. "But you misunderstood one crucial detail." He gestured back towards the study, towards the letter from the lawyer. "He wasn't changing his will to cut Arthur out. He was changing it to put him back in, to give him controlling interest.
